title: A BIOLOGICALLY BASED MODEL OF SPATIAL COGNITION AND WAYFINDING
central_proposition: A biologically based model, utilizing an artificial neural network mechanism of spatial representation, can generate externally valid decision-making behavior in wayfinding tasks within small-scale settings, offering a physiologically plausible alternative to computational process models.

concept_definitions.name: cognitive map
concept_definitions.definition: a psychological process for storing and retrieving spatial information

concept_definitions.name: computer metaphor
concept_definitions.definition: cognitive processes are conceptualized as sets of rules that act on symbolic representations (usually semantic or propositional) of spatial information

concept_definitions.name: Computational Process Modeling (CPM)
concept_definitions.definition: an approach where rules governing cognitive processes models are developed through empirical observations of people engaged in information processing tasks, and reliance on broadly accepted psychological theories of human information processing

concept_definitions.name: biological metaphor
concept_definitions.definition: a view of cognition that is constrained by physiological considerations, attempting to model spatial cognition through lower level, physiologically plausible mechanisms rather than rules

concept_definitions.name: transduction / information pickup
concept_definitions.definition: the process of the translation of perceptual information

concept_definitions.name: activity (in cognitive representation)
concept_definitions.definition: controlled by physiologically based processes that are integral to the representation

concept_definitions.name: choice point
concept_definitions.definition: a location where the user must choose between two or more directions of travel

concept_definitions.name: route representation
concept_definitions.definition: contain topological knowledge about individual places and the way they are connected through experience; the 'travelability' between places

concept_definitions.name: survey representation
concept_definitions.definition: contain knowledge about metrical relations, such as the distance and direction of places in relation to each other

concept_definitions.name: cell assembly
concept_definitions.definition: a group of neurons, or a 'recurrent circuit' which allows activity to persist over time and to spread to other groups of neurons

concept_definitions.name: lateral inhibition
concept_definitions.definition: occurs when two or more highly stimulated nodes compete to cross the threshold for activation, where a highly stimulated node reduces the activity of concurrently stimulated nodes

concept_definitions.name: global inhibition
concept_definitions.definition: functions to increase or decrease the threshold at which any of the nodes in the system can become active

concept_definitions.name: fatigue (neural)
concept_definitions.definition: a process where active nodes cease activity, permitting thought to move on to other content

concept_definitions.name: regional nodes
concept_definitions.definition: higher level, abstract nodes which encode the spatial relations between groups of places

argument_structure: The paper first contrasts the 'computer' and 'biological' metaphors for spatial cognition, developing criteria for analysis based on translation and activity control. It then presents a biologically based neural network model (NAPS-PC) as an exemplar of the biological metaphor, detailing its hierarchical structure, learning mechanisms (contiguity rule), and activity control (fatigue, inhibition). Finally, it describes two experiments comparing the simulation's wayfinding and sketchmap performance to human behavior in real-world settings to evaluate the model's usefulness and validate its predictions.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The biological model (NAPS-PC) proposes that spatial cognition arises from physiologically plausible mechanisms within an associative neural network. Spatial information is represented as a structural analog of the environment, with 'nodes' (cell assemblies) and 'links' (synaptic connections) that transmit activity. Learning occurs through the contiguity rule, where repeated co-activation of places strengthens their associative links. Activity is controlled by neural fatigue (nodes cease activity after stimulation) and inhibition (lateral inhibition for pattern recognition, global inhibition for adjusting activation thresholds), which together focus attention and facilitate decision-making. Hierarchical processing involves lower-level 'place' nodes forming higher-level 'regional' nodes, enabling the development of survey representations. Wayfinding involves stimulating start and goal nodes, with activity spreading until an intermediate subgoal is recognized, effectively reducing the search space.

findings.mechanism: NAPS-PC's physiologically plausible network generates paths based on learned topological connections and activity propagation, which align with human wayfinding behavior only in specific environmental configurations at baseline experience.

findings.mechanism: The model's physiologically plausible mechanisms for spatial representation and activity control effectively simulate human cognitive processes in wayfinding, demonstrating external validity within constrained environments.
findings.quote: These results support the notion that the model is able to predict human wayfinding and sketchmap behavior, at least within relatively small, constrained environments.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Results support the notion that the model is able to predict human wayfinding and sketchmap behavior, at least within relatively small, constrained environments.

findings.consequent: translation of perceptual stimuli from the spatial environment into a usable format
findings.mechanism: Perceptual input is encoded as patterns of activation between groups of neurons, which are generalized to represent events/locations, forming a structural analog of the environment, thus bypassing a separate translation step.
findings.quote: Such a system does not requires a translation process for perceptual information.

findings.consequent: control of activity within the cognitive representation
findings.mechanism: Activity is controlled by integral physiological processes like neural fatigue and inhibition, rather than external rule-based processes, making control intrinsic to the representation.
findings.quote: activity is controlled by physiologically based processes that are integral to the representation.

findings.antecedent: biologically based model utilizing an artificial neural network mechanism
findings.mechanism: Lower-level physiologically based mechanisms generate higher-level cognitive activity, meaning 'rules' are not explicitly specified but arise from the dynamic interactions within the network.
findings.quote: any 'rules' governing psychological processes are emergent from the activity of the system, rather than specified as explicit rules as is the case for computational models.

findings.mechanism: Reliance on a symbolic representational format necessitates an explicit mechanism (a 'proposition generator') to convert sensory input into propositional encodings, which is a complex and unresolved problem.
findings.quote: The problem of translation appears to be unique to the computer metaphor due to its reliance on the symbolic representational format. Such a system requires a 'proposition generator'...

findings.mechanism: Rule-based systems often need a higher-level external mechanism (like 'working memory') to manage rule execution and information flow, which is unlikely to scale effectively in natural systems due to the enormous number of rules required.
findings.quote: the implementation of that theory in the form of a computer simulation does require such a mechanism (Gopal et al., 1989).

findings.antecedent: NAPS-PC with increased experience within an environment
findings.mechanism: The current rudimentary learning mechanism lacks a compensatory component, leading to less efficient searches as the network becomes more complex with increased experience.
findings.quote: its search time performance degrades with increased experience within an environment.

bridge_warrants: The biological model's 'nodes' and 'links' are analogous to groups of neurons and synaptic connections, bridging psychological concepts to neurophysiological mechanisms.

The hierarchical organization of 'place' nodes and 'regional' nodes in the biological model provides a mechanism for the development from route to survey representations, connecting to established theories of cognitive map development.
Neural fatigue and inhibition in the biological model provide a physiologically plausible basis for attention control and decision-making, linking to psychological theories of information processing.
The contiguity rule for learning in the biological model directly implements Hebbian learning principles in a spatial context.
methodological_critiques: The computational process model, with its emphasis on rule-based control systems and symbolic representational format, fails to address the translation of perceptual stimuli into a usable format.

The computational process model implementation (Navigator) requires an external controller ('working memory') to manage cognitive processes, which is unlikely to occur in natural systems due to the enormous number of rules required.

The computational process model is only indirectly physiologically plausible, describing processes like pattern recognition and activation in terms of symbol processing rather than underlying mechanisms.

The CPM approach, while useful for evaluating psychological processes, does not address an explanation of these processes at the physiological level, making it difficult to infer internal system structure.
model_structure: The NAPS-PC model consists of a 'builder' and a 'searcher'. The builder creates a hierarchical associative network (cognitive map) from environmental input (choice point sequences), preserving topological relationships. This network comprises 'nodes' (cell assemblies) and 'links' (synaptic connections) with variable activity levels. The searcher uses this cognitive map to solve wayfinding tasks by propagating activity from start and goal nodes until a subgoal is recognized. Activity is controlled by neural fatigue and lateral/global inhibition. With experience, higher-level 'regional' nodes are created, representing groups of lower-level places, enabling survey-like representations.
limitations: The NAPS-PC model has only a long-term memory structure and a rudimentary learning module.
The NAPS-PC model does not model short-term memory or perceptual processes.
The biological modeling approach is difficult to implement due to its lack of modularity.
Many fundamental questions about the specific mechanisms governing neural activity have not been experimentally validated.
NAPS-PC's search time performance degrades with increased experience within an environment due to the lack of a compensatory learning mechanism.
The current NAPS-PC model is limited to examining topological plan configuration and does not yet incorporate other environmental variables like choice point salience.
